Vignette:
# Arjun's World

Arjun Patel sits at his design workstation in the downtown Minneapolis office where he has worked for eight years, his fingers poised over the keyboard but his attention elsewhere. The morning light filters through the windows facing the street, and when a siren passes—a sound that has become increasingly frequent in his awareness—his shoulders tense and his breath catches. He tells himself it is nothing, that he is being irrational, yet his body does not believe him. He has learned not to fight the sensation. Instead, he waits for it to pass, a familiar knot in his chest that loosens only when the sound fades completely. His colleagues have stopped asking why he sometimes closes his office door or why he is reluctant to attend the weekly team lunches in the downtown core.

Eighteen months ago, Arjun's world fractured in a moment he still cannot fully articulate. He had been driving home from a client meeting on a humid July evening when he was pulled over by police for a broken taillight. The interaction itself began ordinarily—the officer's approach, the request for documents—but what followed remains fragmented in his mind, a sequence of events he knows happened but cannot piece together into a coherent narrative. When he tries to explain it to his wife Priya, his words scatter. He knows the officer's hand moved toward something, knows he felt afraid, knows there was shouting, but when he attempts to reconstruct the moments, the thread breaks. The harder he grasps for clarity, the more elusive it becomes. What he carries most vividly is not the sequence but the overwhelming sensation of betrayal—that a person whose role was to protect had instead become a source of terror, and that this person had been someone he had been taught to trust.

Since that night, Arjun has become hyperaware of uniforms. When he sees a police officer at a coffee shop or walking past his office building, his mind immediately catalogs their position, their direction, whether they have noticed him. He finds himself rehearsing conversations in his head before any interaction with authority—the woman at the DMV, the building manager, even his accountant. He scripts what he will say, anticipating accusations or misunderstandings, preparing justifications. The mental rehearsal has become so habitual that he often does not realize he is doing it until Priya asks why he is so quiet, and he realizes he has been silently running through dialogue for the past twenty minutes.

The smell of burnt rubber or burnt plastic now triggers an immediate sense of danger. Last month, when a colleague microwaved something too long in the office kitchen and a burnt smell drifted through the hallway, Arjun felt his body flood with panic. He had to step outside, telling his manager he needed air. He did not explain why a smell had undone him so completely.

What has changed most noticeably in the past year is Arjun's relationship to the future. He and Priya had been discussing taking a sabbatical, perhaps traveling to India to visit family, but he cannot bring himself to make plans. When she suggests booking flights or looking at dates, something in him resists. He has come to believe that the world is fundamentally unsafe, that planning assumes a future he is no longer certain he will have, or that he deserves to have. The guilt that accompanies memories of that night is intense and irrational—he knows he did nothing wrong, yet when the event surfaces in his mind, he is flooded with a sense of culpability, as though he had somehow caused or invited what happened. This guilt makes planning feel like a betrayal of some unspoken penance he owes.

Priya finally insisted he seek help after finding him, late one night, sitting alone in the dark in their bedroom, unable to articulate why he was there or what he needed. He had called in sick to work three times that week, and his manager had begun to ask questions. Arjun now sits in his first therapy session, exhausted by the effort of holding himself together, hoping that someone might help him understand how a single moment has come to define his entire world, and whether he might ever feel safe again.
